newsitem.title: MONACO: RALLYING-EXCITEMENT RETURNS TO MONTE CARLO CARS.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-EXCITEMENT RETURNS TO MONTE CARLO CARS.

text.p: After 10 years of trying to make rallying cars look just like standard production ones, the sport's officials have cautiously allowed the return of exciting, purpose-built racing machines.

In a bid to attract more manufacturers into the sport, this year's championship, which started on Sunday in Monte Carlo, features new vehicles with an aggressive silhouette called World Rally Cars (WRC).
In the past constructors have been put off by the unnecessary expense of having to build 2,500 models identical to their racing car which, by their nature, rarely found buyers in the high street.
That cost has now been reduced by the decision to allow them the chance to take a standard showroom model and modify it.

The only stipulation is that they must now build 25,000 models. It sounds as though it should be more expensive but the fact that they are standard cars makes them more saleable and a better investment.
Only Subaru and Ford are fielding WRC cars in Monte Carlo as the old group A cars are still allowed to compete.

Mitsubishi will rely on an improved version of the Lancer in which Finn Tommi Makinen won the world championship title last year but a new Carisma WRC car should make its debut in the next round in February in Sweden.
Toyota, Skoda and Audi are also planning to launch WRC cars before the end of the season while non-works competitors will also be able to benefit.
Manufacturers must work on the basis of a two-litre, family saloon car to which they can add four-wheel drive and a turbocharger.
Externally, wider wings, which make the suspension system more efficient and give the car a more exciting look, are allowed as well as rear ailerons.
The new cars look like the extremely powerful but equally dangerous group B prototypes which were banned in 1987.
But safeguards, such as a minimum body length and a maximum width, have been included. The new cars will have to be fitted with a 34-mm restrictor reducing the effect of the turbocharger.
"The aggressive looks, the ailerons and the wider wings might evoke the group B cars but the new cars are much safer and much more reliable," said Ford Motorsport technical director Philip Dunabin.
Now everybody is waiting to see if the WRCs are faster than the group A cars.
"They will surely be a little faster on dry asphalt but on other terrains the difference will probably not be very significant," predicted former world champion Didier Auriol .
Belgian Freddy Loix clocked the fastest time of Sunday's wet, first timed stage of the rally in a group A Toyota Celica.
Spaniard Carlos Sainz, in his Ford Escort WRC, was two seconds slower.
